name: Ogbogolo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kari, Ethelbert Emmanuel. 2017. Central Delta languages: An overview. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics 47: 1-26. doi:10.5774/47-0-213 (open access).
catalog_locator: p. 11, sec. 3.4 'Tone' (between the p.10 and p.11 journal footers); Ogbogolo tone-marked forms at Table 11b p. 16, ex. (16) p. 20 and ex. (32) p. 22; Ogbogolo's data sources stated on p. 3 and p. 6.
catalog_quote: Alex (1989:24) remarks that “all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system”. These tones are low tone, which is marked with a grave accent (̀), and high tone, which is marked with an acute accent (´). There is also a downstep phenomenon in these languages. The downstep is marked with a small arrow pointing downwards (ꜜ) between two high-toned syllables. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Oḍual and Ogbrọnụagum. ... Like in lexical items, tone can distinguish grammatical constructions in Central Delta languages. [p. 22, ex. (32), Ogbogolo: Olibie 1994:55] óꜜdó nǝ̀ ǝ́dí nǝ́ ǝ́ɡí òlòɡì òtù. Odo CM enter CM go inside house “Odo entered into the house.”
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

The quoted passage is at p. 11, sec. 3.4 'Tone' (the text) and matches word for word: 'Alex (1989:24) remarks that "all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system". These tones are low tone.. grave accent.. high tone.. acute accent.. downstep.. marked with a small arrow pointing downwards ( ꜜ) between two high-toned syllables. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum.' a full-text search for stress/accent confirms 0 occurrences of 'stress' in the whole paper; 'accent' occurs only as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogbogolo, like all Central Delta languages, is treated as a two-level tone language (H, L) with downstep; every vowel (and syllabic nasal) bears tone. No source seen says anything about word stress or accent placement in Ogbogolo.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone statement is a family-level generalisation illustrated only with Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum forms, not Ogbogolo forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical and grammatical tone (word level); the statement is second-hand (Kari quoting Alex 1989) and generic to Central Delta, applied to Ogbogolo by membership. Nothing on citation-form prominence or phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same single-town language Ogbogolo/Obogolo (ogbo1242, ISO ogg), Ahoada West LGA, Rivers State (Blench 2008; Kari 2017 Table 3 instead gives 'Bayelsa State: Yenagoa LGA', apparently an error carried from Ethnologue mapping). The quoted tone statement is a Central Delta family-level generalisation (Kari 2017 quoting Alex 1989), not an Ogbogolo-specific observation, and it says nothing about stress.

tone_statements.citation: Kari, Ethelbert Emmanuel. 2019. The languages of Rivers State of Nigeria: An overview. Marang: Journal of Language and Literature 31: 1-22. Gaborone: University of Botswana.
tone_statements.quote: Tone is another interesting phonological characteristic of Rivers State languages. In all Rivers State languages, the pitch of the voice can be used to distinguish words, phrases and sentences whose segmental compositions are otherwise the same. ... The tones that are attested in Rivers State languages include high (́), mid (ˉ), low (̀), and downstepped-high tone (a phonetically lowered high tone in the environment of a preceding floating low tone represented with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned syllables σ́ꜜσ́).
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, sec. 5.1 'Phonological Profile of Rivers State Languages' (section runs pp. 9-11; tone-marking footnote on p. 9)
tone_statements.summary: Areal/state-level statement only: every Rivers State language (Ogbogolo included by enumeration) has lexical and grammatical tone; the tones attested across these languages are H, M, L and downstepped H, downstep arising from a preceding floating L between two H syllables; tone also marks statement vs question (Degema). No Ogbogolo-specific tone inventory, TBU or rule is given; combined with Kari…

sources.note: Nothing: the word 'stress' does not occur in the paper. Sec. 3 (phonological overview) covers vowels, consonants (Ogbogolo credited with 27 consonants after Olibie 1994 / Francstan 1995), syllable structure and, in sec. 3.4 (p. 11), tone: quoting Alex (1989:24) that 'all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system' (H, L) plus downstep, tone anchored on vowels and syllabic nasals; tone examples given only for Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum. Ogbogolo data throughout are second-hand from two unpublished UniPort long essays.
Bibliography only: Glottolog's most extensive descriptions = Francstan 1995, Olibie 1994 (phonology or text collection), Thomas 1914 (wordlist).

sources.note: Sec. 5.1 states that in all Rivers State languages pitch distinguishes words, phrases and sentences (lexical and grammatical tone); tones attested across the state's languages are high, mid, low and downstepped high (downstep = H lowered after a preceding floating L); statement/question pairs distinguished by tone (Degema ex. 7); footnote p. 9: low tone left unmarked in the paper's data. No word stress or accent is mentioned anywhere in the paper (0 occurrences of 'stress'). Ogbogolo-specific content is segmental only (20 vowels incl. long vowels; verbal extensions as suffixes).
